stem: A team's task always follows the same fixed steps: translate a document, check the translation against a glossary, then format it. They want predictable, consistent results. What should they build?

choices.text: A workflow: LLMs and tools orchestrated via predefined code paths
choices.reason: Correct: workflows offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks like this one.

choices.text: An autonomous agent, because agents always perform better on any task
choices.reason: Anthropic recommends the simplest solution possible; agents fit when flexibility and model-driven decisions are needed.

choices.text: An agent, because agentic systems cost less and respond faster
choices.reason: The reverse: agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance.

choices.text: A multi-agent system with one specialized agent assigned to each step
choices.reason: More moving parts adds complexity without need; increase complexity only when simpler solutions fall short.

takeaway: Fixed, well-defined steps → **workflow**; open-ended problems needing model-driven decisions → **agent**.
explanation: The rule is to pick the simplest solution that works: workflows run LLMs and tools through **predefined code paths**, which buys predictability and consistency. Notice the stem says the steps are **always the same** and the team wants consistent results, so nothing needs model-driven decisions. Option B is the tempting trap, but agents fit when you need flexibility, not because they always perform better. Option C reverses the trade-off (agents often cost more latency and money), and D adds moving parts without need.
mnemonic: Fixed path → workflow; open path → agent.

stem: Your coding agent usually finishes its task, but occasionally keeps calling tools without converging. Which safeguard, commonly included in agent designs according to Anthropic's guidance, helps you keep control?

choices.text: Hide tool results from the agent so it can't get stuck on them
choices.reason: Agents need ground truth from the environment, such as tool results, at each step to assess progress.

choices.text: Trust the model to stop; agent tasks always terminate on completion
choices.reason: Tasks often end on completion, but the guidance notes it's also common to include stopping conditions to maintain control.

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` so each turn can finish its thought
choices.reason: `max_tokens` caps a single response's length; it doesn't bound how many loop iterations run.

choices.text: A stopping condition such as a maximum number of iterations
choices.reason: Correct: it's common to include stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations, to maintain control.

takeaway: Add a **stopping condition** (e.g. a maximum number of iterations) to keep control of an agent loop, and feed it real tool results each step.
explanation: Agent loops usually end when the task is done, but Anthropic's guidance notes it is common to add a **stopping condition** such as a maximum number of iterations to keep control. The stem's detail is that the agent *occasionally* fails to converge, so you need a bound on the loop itself. Option B is the trap: tasks often end on completion, but that is no guarantee. Option C only caps one response's length, not the number of iterations, and A removes the tool results an agent needs to judge its progress.
mnemonic: Cap the loop to keep control.

stem: Your team is choosing a first project for a multi-agent system (a lead agent plus parallel subagents). Based on Anthropic's experience building its Research feature, which task is the best fit?

choices.text: A coding task where every change depends on context the other agents also need
choices.reason: Domains where all agents must share the same context, or with many dependencies between agents, are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today.

choices.text: High-volume, low-value support tickets, to cut the tokens spent on each one
choices.reason: Multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats, so they need tasks valuable enough to pay for the increased performance.

choices.text: A breadth-first research question with many independent directions
choices.reason: Correct: multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries that pursue multiple independent directions simultaneously.

choices.text: A simple fact lookup that has one short, well-defined answer
choices.reason: The post's scaling rules say simple fact-finding needs just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls; more agents would be overinvestment.

takeaway: Multi-agent pays off on **valuable, parallelizable** work; shared context and tight dependencies between agents are a poor fit today.
explanation: Multi-agent systems shine on **breadth-first** work that splits into **independent directions** a lead agent can farm out in parallel, and the task must be valuable enough to pay for the extra tokens. Option C matches both. Option A is the tempting one because coding feels complex, but agents that all need the same context or depend heavily on each other are a poor fit today. Option B fails on value (about 15x the tokens of a chat), and D is a one-agent fact lookup where more agents would be overinvestment.

source.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

stem: A manager assumes that splitting a task across parallel subagents will lower the token bill, since each subagent does less. What does Anthropic's data from its multi-agent research system suggest?

choices.text: Token use drops, because each subagent works in a smaller, focused context
choices.reason: Each subagent has its own context window, but the total grows: multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats.

choices.text: Token use rises sharply, so the task's value must justify it
choices.reason: Correct: multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats, so they need tasks whose value is high enough to pay for the increased performance.

choices.text: Token use stays about the same; only the wall-clock time goes down
choices.reason: Parallelism did cut research time, but these architectures burn through tokens fast; the total does not stay the same.

choices.text: Token use matches a single agent, about 4× a chat
choices.reason: About 4× is the figure for single agents versus chats; multi-agent systems use about 15×.

takeaway: Multi-agent systems trade **tokens** (about 15× a chat) for performance, so save them for high-value tasks.
explanation: The manager's intuition is backwards: each subagent has its own context window, so the **total** token count grows, to about 15x a chat in Anthropic's data. That is why the task's value must justify the spend, which is Option B. Option A is the trap, mistaking smaller per-agent contexts for a smaller bill. Option C is half right (parallelism did cut research time) but the tokens do not stay flat, and D quotes the about 4x figure that applies to single agents, not multi-agent systems.

source.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

stem: Your lead research agent gives subagents short instructions like "research the semiconductor shortage". Two subagents end up running the same searches while an important angle goes uncovered. What change does Anthropic recommend?

choices.text: Give each subagent an objective, output format, tool/source guidance and clear boundaries
choices.reason: Correct: each subagent needs these; without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information.

choices.text: Spawn more subagents with the same short instructions so the missing angle gets covered by chance
choices.reason: More agents with vague briefs just duplicate more work; early agents even spawned 50 subagents for simple queries.

choices.text: Have all subagents share one context window so they can see each other's searches as they work
choices.reason: Subagents are meant to have their own context windows; that separation of concerns reduces path dependency and enables independent investigations.

choices.text: Keep the short instructions and move subagents to a larger model
choices.reason: The failure came from instructions vague enough that subagents misinterpreted the task; the fix is teaching the orchestrator how to delegate.

takeaway: Teach the orchestrator to delegate: every subagent gets an **objective, output format, tools and boundaries**.
explanation: The failure is in delegation: a vague brief like "research the semiconductor shortage" let subagents misread the task, duplicate searches and leave gaps. Anthropic's fix is teaching the orchestrator to give each subagent an **objective, output format, tool/source guidance and clear boundaries** (Option A). Option B is tempting because more agents seem to add coverage, but vague briefs just multiply duplicate work. Option C undoes the separate context windows that enable independent investigation, and D changes the model while keeping the vague instructions.

source.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

stem: Your coding agent works across many context windows. Each new session starts with no memory, has to guess what happened, and spends time getting the app working again. Which harness change did Anthropic find effective?

choices.text: Rely on the SDK's compaction alone to carry all context between sessions
choices.reason: Compaction isn't sufficient on its own; it doesn't always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent.

choices.text: Prompt the agent to build the whole app in one session
choices.reason: Trying to one-shot the app led the model to run out of context mid-implementation, leaving a half-implemented, undocumented feature.

choices.text: Let each new session judge from the code whether the project is done
choices.reason: That is a known failure mode: a later agent sees that progress has been made and declares the job done.

choices.text: Maintain a progress file and git log every session reads and updates
choices.reason: Correct: a claude-progress.txt file alongside the git history lets agents quickly understand the state of work in a fresh context window.

takeaway: Bridge sessions with **artifacts**: a progress file plus git history that every new session reads first and updates before it ends.
explanation: The symptom is that each fresh context window starts blind, so the fix is a durable **artifact** the next session reads first: a progress file plus the git log, updated every session (Option D). Option A is the tempting trap, because compaction sounds like it carries context forward, but on its own it does not always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent. Option B led the model to run out of context mid-feature, and C is the known failure mode where a later agent sees progress and declares the job done.

diagram.caption: A typical coding-agent session in Anthropic's harness.

stem: Midway through a long project, a fresh session of your coding agent sees that many features exist and declares the whole app finished, though much is missing. Which fix matches Anthropic's long-running agent harness?

choices.text: A Markdown checklist of features that agents may freely reword and reorganize as they work
choices.reason: The harness uses JSON because the model is less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite JSON files than Markdown files.

choices.text: A JSON feature list, all initially failing, editable only via each `passes` field
choices.reason: Correct: every feature starts as failing and agents may only change its passes status, giving a clear outline of what full functionality looks like.

choices.text: Let agents remove or edit tests that keep a feature from being marked passing
choices.reason: The harness forbids this with strongly worded instructions: removing or editing tests could lead to missing or buggy functionality.

choices.text: Mark a feature done as soon as its unit tests and curl checks pass
choices.reason: Unit tests or curl commands alone missed features that didn't work end-to-end; the harness marks features passing only after careful testing.

takeaway: Guard against early victory with a **feature list** that starts all-failing and flips to passing only after careful testing.
explanation: The problem is a fresh session judging "done" from what exists. The harness counters this with a **JSON feature list** where every feature starts as failing and agents may only flip its `passes` field, so the full scope stays visible (Option B). Option A is the closest trap, but the harness picks JSON because the model is less likely to inappropriately rewrite it than Markdown. Option C invites missing or buggy functionality, and D fails because unit tests or curl checks alone missed features that didn't work end-to-end.

stem: Your coding agent works for several hours, far beyond one context window, building the product up step by step and checking off each defined stage before starting the next. Which long-horizon technique does Anthropic's context engineering post say excels for this kind of task?

choices.text: Compaction, which keeps conversational flow for heavy back-and-forth
choices.reason: Compaction maintains conversational flow for tasks requiring extensive back-and-forth, which is not what defines this task.

choices.text: A multi-agent architecture, built for research where parallel exploration pays off
choices.reason: Multi-agent architectures handle complex research and analysis where parallel exploration pays dividends.

choices.text: Structured note-taking, persisting notes outside the context window
choices.reason: Correct: the post says note-taking excels for iterative development with clear milestones.

choices.text: Waiting for a model with a larger context window
choices.reason: For the foreseeable future, context windows of all sizes are likely to face context pollution and information relevance concerns.

takeaway: Match the technique to the task: **compaction** for back-and-forth, **notes** for milestones, **sub-agents** for parallel research.
explanation: The post matches long-horizon techniques to task shape. The stem's key detail is **iterative development with clear milestones** (checking off each defined stage), which is where **structured note-taking** outside the context window excels (Option C). Option A is the tempting one since compaction also handles long runs, but it is suited to heavy back-and-forth conversation, not milestone-driven building. Option B fits parallel research, and D fails because context windows of all sizes are likely to face pollution and relevance concerns.

source.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

stem: A team wants an autonomous agent to answer customer questions from their help-center articles. A single well-prompted call with retrieved articles already answers most questions correctly. What does Anthropic's guidance suggest?

choices.text: Keep optimizing the single LLM call with retrieval and examples
choices.reason: Correct: find the simplest solution possible; for many applications, optimizing single LLM calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough.

choices.text: Build the agent anyway, since agents are cheaper and faster
choices.reason: Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, so they are not the cheaper, faster option.

choices.text: Build a multi-agent system so every question gets several perspectives
choices.reason: Add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes; here the simple setup already works.

choices.text: Wrap it in a fixed workflow of many chained LLM calls to be safe
choices.reason: Workflows suit well-defined multi-step tasks, but the guidance says the simplest solution might mean not building agentic systems at all.

takeaway: If one optimized LLM call works, stop there: add agentic complexity only **when simpler solutions fall short**.
explanation: Anthropic's rule is to find the **simplest solution possible** and add complexity only when simpler solutions fall short. Notice the stem says one well-prompted call with retrieval **already answers most questions correctly**, so keep optimizing that call (Option A). Option D is the subtle trap: a fixed workflow sounds safe, but the guidance says the simplest solution might mean not building agentic systems at all. Option B gets the trade-off backwards, and C adds complexity that has not shown it improves outcomes.

stem: You want to embed an agent with built-in file, shell and web tools, plus permissions and hooks, inside your own Python service, running in a process you operate. Which Anthropic option fits?

choices.text: The Client SDK, calling the Claude API directly
choices.reason: The Client SDK gives direct access to the Claude API, but you write the tool loop yourself or use its beta tool runner.

choices.text: The Claude Agent SDK
choices.reason: Correct: it's a library that runs the Claude Code binary in your application, with built-in tools, permissions, sessions and hooks.

choices.text: The Claude Code CLI in an interactive terminal
choices.reason: The CLI is the terminal interface built for daily interactive use, not a library you embed in a service.

choices.text: Claude Managed Agents
choices.reason: Managed Agents is for having Anthropic host the agent, configured through the Claude API, rather than a process you operate.

takeaway: Embed Claude Code's agent in your own process → **Agent SDK**; raw API calls → Client SDK; Anthropic-hosted → Managed Agents.
explanation: The deciding details are **built-in file, shell and web tools, permissions and hooks**, embedded in **your own** Python service in a process you operate. That is the Claude Agent SDK, a library that runs the Claude Code binary inside your app (Option B). Option A is the tempting trap because it is also a library, but the Client SDK gives raw API access and leaves the tool loop to you or its beta tool runner. Option C is the interactive terminal, and D has Anthropic host the agent rather than you.

stem: Your SDK agent runs with `max_turns=30`. On a large refactor, the final `ResultMessage` has subtype `error_max_turns`, and your code reads its `result` field and gets nothing. What should you do?

choices.text: Read `result` anyway; on a max-turns stop it holds the partial answer so far
choices.reason: The `result` field is only present on the `success` variant, so always check the subtype before reading it.

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` so each turn can do more work before the cap
choices.reason: `max_tokens` is the output token limit; this loop ended because it hit the cap on tool-use turns, a different limit.

choices.text: Check the subtype first, then resume the session with a higher turn limit
choices.reason: Correct: `result` exists only on `success`, while every result carries `session_id`, so you can resume with a higher limit.

choices.text: Remove the turn limit entirely, since unlimited loops suit production best
choices.reason: The caps default to no limit, but open-ended prompts can run long; setting a budget is a good default for production agents.

takeaway: Check `ResultMessage.subtype` before reading `result`; after `error_max_turns`, **resume** the session rather than start over.
explanation: In the SDK, `result` exists **only on the `success` variant**, so you must check `subtype` before reading it; every result still carries a `session_id`. After `error_max_turns`, the right move is to resume that session with a higher turn limit (Option C). Option A is the trap: it assumes `result` holds a partial answer, which it does not. Option B confuses `max_tokens` (output length) with the cap on tool-use turns, and D drops a budget that is a good default for production agents.

stem: Your CI agent must run in `bypassPermissions` mode. You set `allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep"]`, expecting a read-only agent, but it still ran `Bash` commands. How do you block Bash while keeping the mode?

choices.text: Add a `canUseTool` callback that denies Bash
choices.reason: Calls auto-approved by `bypassPermissions` skip `canUseTool`, so permission checks placed there are silently bypassed.

choices.text: Add only safe commands, like `Bash(ls *)`, to `allowed_tools`
choices.reason: Allow rules only pre-approve. Other calls still fall through to the permission mode, where `bypassPermissions` approves them.

choices.text: Nothing works, because bypassPermissions ignores deny rules too
choices.reason: Deny rules are checked before the permission mode; a matching deny rule blocks the tool even in `bypassPermissions` mode.

choices.text: Add `Bash` to `disallowed_tools`
choices.reason: Correct: `allowed_tools` does not constrain `bypassPermissions`, but a bare `disallowed_tools` entry removes Bash from the request.

takeaway: `allowed_tools` **pre-approves**; it does not restrict. To block a tool under `bypassPermissions`, use `disallowed_tools`.
explanation: The principle: `allowed_tools` only **pre-approves**; it does not restrict. Under `bypassPermissions`, unlisted calls fall through to the mode, which approves them, so Bash still ran. Deny rules are checked **before** the permission mode, so adding `Bash` to `disallowed_tools` blocks it while keeping the mode (Option D). Option A is the tempting trap, because calls auto-approved by `bypassPermissions` skip `canUseTool` entirely. Option B is another allow rule with the same fall-through problem, and C is false since deny rules still apply.

stem: Your Agent SDK app must stop the agent from writing to `.env` files, and tell Claude why so it avoids retrying. Which hook setup fits?

choices.text: A `PreToolUse` hook on `Write|Edit` returning a deny decision and a reason
choices.reason: Correct: PreToolUse fires before the tool runs and can block it; `permissionDecisionReason` tells the model why, so it avoids retrying.

choices.text: A `PostToolUse` hook on `Write|Edit` that inspects the file right after the write
choices.reason: PostToolUse fires on the tool execution result, after the write has already happened; its example use is an audit trail.

choices.text: A `PreToolUse` hook that returns an async output while it checks the file path
choices.reason: Async outputs cannot block, modify or inject context, because the agent has already moved on; use them only for side effects.

choices.text: A `Stop` hook that reverts any `.env` changes when the agent finishes its run
choices.reason: Stop fires when agent execution stops, too late to prevent the write; its example use is saving session state before exit.

takeaway: To **prevent** a tool action, deny it in `PreToolUse` with a reason; a `PostToolUse` hook runs after the tool already ran.
explanation: To **prevent** an action, a hook must run before the tool and be able to block it: that is `PreToolUse`, returning a deny decision plus a `permissionDecisionReason` so Claude knows why and avoids retrying (Option A). Option B is the tempting trap, but `PostToolUse` fires on the result, after the `.env` write already happened. Option C uses an async output, which cannot block because the agent has already moved on, and D's `Stop` hook fires only when the run ends, far too late.

diagram.caption: A PreToolUse deny stops the call before it runs.

source.title: Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks

stem: Your custom Agent SDK tool calls an inventory API. When the API returns a 503, the handler throws, and Claude sees only a raw exception message it can't act on. What should you change?

choices.text: Nothing; an uncaught handler error ends the query, which is the safest outcome
choices.reason: A handler error doesn't stop the agent loop: the in-process MCP server converts it to an error result and the loop continues.

choices.text: Catch it and return the error text as a normal, successful tool result
choices.reason: Without `isError`, Claude would treat the failure as a normal result instead of knowing the tool failed.

choices.text: Catch it and return `isError: true` with what failed and what to try
choices.reason: Correct: returning isError lets you compose the message Claude reads, adding context the raw exception lacks, such as what to try instead.

choices.text: Mark the tool `readOnlyHint: true` so the SDK retries it after failures
choices.reason: `readOnlyHint` controls whether the tool can be called in parallel with other read-only tools; it adds no retries.

takeaway: Handler errors don't stop the loop; return **`isError: true`** with an actionable message so Claude can retry or adapt.
explanation: A handler error does not stop the agent loop; the in-process MCP server turns it into an error result and the loop continues. The issue is that Claude only sees an unhelpful raw exception, so catch it and return `isError: true` with a message you write: what failed and what to try (Option C). Option B is the tempting near-miss, but without `isError` Claude treats the failure as a normal result. Option A misreads how errors behave, and D's `readOnlyHint` governs parallel calls, not retries.

stem: Your main agent spends ten turns finding a failing test and its file path, then delegates the fix to a `test-fixer` subagent (not a fork). The subagent starts searching from scratch. Why, and what is the fix?

choices.text: It inherited too much parent history; set a smaller `maxTurns`
choices.reason: A non-fork subagent gets none of the parent's conversation history, and `maxTurns` only caps how many turns it takes.

choices.text: It sees only the Agent tool's prompt; put the path and error in it
choices.reason: Correct: the Agent tool's prompt string is the only content passed from parent to subagent, so include file paths, errors and decisions.

choices.text: It lacks the parent's system prompt; copy it into the subagent's definition
choices.reason: The facts it needs came from the parent's turns, not its system prompt; the subagent uses its own system prompt by design.

choices.text: It needs more tools; remove its `tools` restriction
choices.reason: Tool access controls what the subagent can do, not what it knows; the parent's findings only arrive through the prompt.

takeaway: Subagents start fresh: pass what they need **in the Agent tool's prompt**; only their final message returns to the parent.
explanation: A non-fork subagent starts fresh: the **Agent tool's prompt string** is the only content passed from parent to subagent, so the ten turns of findings never reached it. The fix is to put the file path, error and decisions in that prompt (Option B). Option C is the tempting trap, but the needed facts came from the parent's turns, not its system prompt, and the subagent uses its own by design. Option A is backwards (it inherits no history), and D changes what the subagent can do, not what it knows.

stem: You are adopting Claude Managed Agents. You want to define the model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers and skills once, then reuse them across many runs. Which resource do you create and reference by ID?

choices.text: An environment
choices.reason: An environment configures where sessions run: an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox, or a self-hosted sandbox on your own infrastructure.

choices.text: A session
choices.reason: A session is a running agent instance within an environment, performing a specific task and generating outputs.

choices.text: An event
choices.reason: Events are messages exchanged between your application and the agent, such as user turns, tool results and status updates.

choices.text: An agent
choices.reason: Correct: an agent holds the model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers and skills; you create it once and reference it by ID across sessions.

takeaway: Managed Agents: **agent** = model, prompt and tools; **environment** = where it runs; **session** = one run; **events** = messages.
explanation: Managed Agents splits configuration into resources. The stem asks for **model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers and skills** defined once and reused across runs: that bundle is an **agent**, referenced by ID across sessions (Option D). Option A is the tempting one because it also sounds like reusable setup, but an environment only configures where sessions run (cloud or self-hosted sandbox). A session (B) is one running instance, and events (C) are the messages exchanged with the agent.

stem: Your pipeline writes a document outline, checks that it meets required criteria, then writes the full document from it. The steps never change, and you'll accept extra latency for accuracy. Which pattern is this?

choices.text: Prompt chaining, with a programmatic gate after the outline
choices.reason: Correct: chaining decomposes a task into fixed steps, each call processing the previous output, with checks on intermediate steps.

choices.text: Routing, classifying the request and sending it to a specialized follow-up prompt
choices.reason: Routing classifies an input and sends it to a specialized follow-up task; here every input goes through the same fixed steps.

choices.text: Orchestrator-workers, with a central LLM delegating the outline and writing steps
choices.reason: Orchestrator-workers fits tasks where you can't predict the subtasks; these steps are fixed in advance.

choices.text: An autonomous agent that decides its own steps and tools in a loop
choices.reason: Agents suit open-ended problems where you can't hardcode a fixed path; this path is fixed.

takeaway: Fixed, sequential steps with checks in between → **prompt chaining**, which makes each LLM call an easier task.
explanation: Prompt chaining decomposes a task into **fixed sequential steps**, each call processing the previous output, with checks (gates) on intermediate results. The stem's clues are that the steps **never change**, there is a check on the outline, and you accept extra latency for accuracy, so Option A fits. Option C is the tempting trap because it also splits work, but orchestrator-workers is for subtasks you can't predict in advance. Routing (B) sends inputs down different paths, and an agent (D) suits paths you can't hardcode.

diagram.caption: Prompt chaining with a gate between steps.

stem: Your support bot handles general questions, refund requests and technical support with one prompt. Every time you tune it for refunds, technical answers get worse. Which workflow does Anthropic suggest?

choices.text: Parallelization with voting, running each query several times for diverse outputs
choices.reason: Voting runs the same task several times to get diverse outputs; it doesn't separate distinct query types.

choices.text: Evaluator-optimizer, with a second call critiquing and refining each reply in a loop
choices.reason: Evaluator-optimizer refines a response through feedback in a loop; it doesn't stop tuning for one category from hurting another.

choices.text: Routing: classify each query and send it to a specialized prompt and tools
choices.reason: Correct: routing allows separation of concerns; without it, optimizing for one kind of input can hurt performance on other inputs.

choices.text: Prompt chaining, passing each query through the same fixed sequence of calls
choices.reason: Chaining runs the same fixed sequence of steps on every input, so all query types would still share the same prompts.

takeaway: Distinct input categories fighting over one prompt → **route** each one to its own specialized path.
explanation: The tell is that tuning the one prompt for refunds makes technical answers worse: distinct input categories are fighting over one prompt. **Routing** classifies each query and sends it to a specialized prompt and tools, giving separation of concerns (Option C). Option B is tempting because refining replies sounds like better quality, but an evaluator-optimizer loop doesn't keep one category's tuning from hurting another. Voting (A) repeats the same task, and chaining (D) still runs every query through the same prompts.

stem: You want higher confidence that a piece of code has no vulnerabilities. You plan to run several different prompts that each review the same code and flag any problem they find. Which workflow is this, and which variation?

choices.text: Parallelization, sectioning
choices.reason: Sectioning breaks a task into independent subtasks; here every prompt does the same task on the same code.

choices.text: Orchestrator-workers
choices.reason: In orchestrator-workers a central LLM decides the subtasks dynamically; here the reviews are fixed in advance.

choices.text: Prompt chaining
choices.reason: Chaining feeds each call the previous call's output in sequence; these reviews run independently of each other.

choices.text: Parallelization, voting
choices.reason: Correct: voting runs the same task multiple times for diverse outputs, as when several prompts review code for vulnerabilities.

takeaway: Same task, several runs → **voting**; different independent subtasks → **sectioning**. Both aggregate outputs programmatically.
explanation: Parallelization has two variations: **sectioning** splits a task into different independent subtasks, while **voting** runs the same task several times for diverse outputs. Here several prompts each review the **same code** for the same goal, flagging problems, which is voting (Option D). Option A is the closest trap since it is also parallelization, but sectioning would give each prompt a different subtask. Orchestrator-workers (B) decides subtasks dynamically, and chaining (C) runs calls in sequence rather than independently.

stem: Your coding tool gets requests like "rename this API everywhere". The number of files and the change in each depend on the request, so you cannot list the subtasks in advance. Which workflow fits best?

choices.text: Parallelization, sectioning the work into a fixed set of subtasks
choices.reason: Sectioning looks similar, but its subtasks are predefined; here they depend on the specific input.

choices.text: Orchestrator-workers
choices.reason: Correct: a central LLM dynamically breaks down the task, delegates to workers and synthesizes results, since subtasks aren't predefined.

choices.text: Routing to a specialized prompt per file type
choices.reason: Routing sends an input to one follow-up task by category; it doesn't break one task into an unknown number of subtasks.

choices.text: Prompt chaining with one step per file
choices.reason: Chaining suits tasks that decompose cleanly into fixed subtasks, which this one does not.

takeaway: Can't predict the subtasks? An **orchestrator** decides them per input; parallelization needs them defined in advance.
explanation: The deciding detail is that the number of files and the change in each **depend on the request**, so subtasks can't be listed in advance. Orchestrator-workers handles that: a central LLM breaks the task down per input, delegates to workers and synthesizes results (Option B). Option A is the tempting look-alike, but sectioning requires predefined subtasks. Routing (C) sends an input to one follow-up path rather than splitting it, and chaining (D) needs a task that decomposes cleanly into fixed steps.

diagram.caption: Orchestrator-workers: subtasks are decided per input.

stem: You translate literary texts. First drafts miss nuances, but a second model can reliably critique them against clear criteria, and revising on that feedback measurably improves them. Which workflow fits?

choices.text: Routing between translation models
choices.reason: Routing picks one specialized path per input; it has no feedback loop to refine a draft.

choices.text: Parallelization with sectioning
choices.reason: Sectioning splits a task into independent subtasks; it doesn't iterate on one draft using critiques.

choices.text: Evaluator-optimizer
choices.reason: Correct: one call generates while another evaluates and gives feedback in a loop, which fits clear criteria and measurable gains from refinement.

choices.text: Prompt chaining with fixed translate, then format steps
choices.reason: Chaining runs each fixed step once; it has no loop in which an evaluator's feedback drives further revisions.

takeaway: Clear criteria plus feedback that measurably improves drafts → an **evaluator-optimizer** loop.
explanation: An evaluator-optimizer loop fits when there are **clear evaluation criteria** and feedback **measurably improves** the output: one call drafts, another critiques, and the draft is revised in a loop. The stem gives both conditions (a second model critiques reliably, and revisions measurably help), so Option C fits. Option D is the tempting trap since a translate-then-format pipeline sounds natural, but chaining runs each step once with no feedback loop. Routing (A) and sectioning (B) also lack any iterative refinement.

stem: A new team plans to adopt an agent framework before writing any code, so they never need to look at raw prompts or API responses. What does Anthropic's Building effective agents post advise?

choices.text: Start with LLM APIs directly; if using a framework, understand its code
choices.reason: Correct: many patterns take a few lines of code, and incorrect assumptions about what's under the hood are a common source of customer error.

choices.text: Always use a framework, since it hides prompts and responses you never need to see
choices.reason: Hiding prompts is the risk: extra abstraction can obscure the underlying prompts and responses, making them harder to debug.

choices.text: Avoid frameworks entirely; Anthropic says they don't work
choices.reason: The post says frameworks make it easy to get started by simplifying low-level tasks; the caution is to understand them, not to ban them.

choices.text: Choose the framework with the most abstraction layers for production
choices.reason: The advice runs the other way: reduce abstraction layers and build with basic components as you move to production.

takeaway: Start with **direct API calls**; frameworks help you start fast, but know what is under the hood and trim layers for production.
explanation: The advice is to **start with LLM APIs directly**, since many patterns take a few lines of code, and if you do use a framework, understand what's under the hood, because wrong assumptions about it are a common source of customer error (Option A). The stem's goal of never looking at prompts or responses is exactly the risk, which makes Option B the trap: hidden prompts are harder to debug. Option C overcorrects (frameworks do help you start), and D is backwards, since production calls for fewer abstraction layers.

stem: A headless CI agent built on the Agent SDK should run `Read`, `Glob` and `Grep` without prompting, and any call that would need approval must be denied outright rather than relying on there being no `canUseTool` callback. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Those three in `allowedTools`, with `permissionMode: "bypassPermissions"`
choices.reason: `allowed_tools` does not constrain `bypassPermissions`: unlisted tools fall through to the mode, which approves them, Bash and Write included.

choices.text: Those three in `allowedTools`, with `permissionMode: "acceptEdits"`
choices.reason: `acceptEdits` auto-approves file edits and filesystem commands such as `mkdir`, `rm` and `mv` in the working directory, so the surface grows.

choices.text: Those three in `allowedTools` only, leaving the mode at `default`
choices.reason: In `default` mode, unlisted calls that need approval fall through to `canUseTool`; the docs suggest `dontAsk` for a hard deny instead.

choices.text: Those three in `allowedTools`, with `permissionMode: "dontAsk"`
choices.reason: Correct: listed tools are approved, and every other call that would prompt is denied without calling `canUseTool`.

takeaway: For a fixed, locked-down tool surface, pair `allowedTools` with **`dontAsk`**: anything that would prompt is denied instead.
explanation: The stem wants two things: listed read tools approved without prompts, and **every other call that would prompt denied outright**, without depending on a missing `canUseTool`. `allowedTools` plus `permissionMode: "dontAsk"` does exactly that (Option D). Option C is the tempting trap, since leaving `default` looks restrictive, but unlisted calls then fall through to `canUseTool` instead of a hard deny. Option A lets `bypassPermissions` approve everything unlisted, and B's `acceptEdits` widens the surface with file edits and commands.

stem: Your Python app drives an agent with `ClaudeSDKClient` in `default` mode. Once the user has reviewed Claude's first proposed changes and approved the approach, later file edits in the same session should run without prompts. What should you do?

choices.text: End the session and start a new query with `permission_mode="acceptEdits"`
choices.reason: Not needed: the mode can change during a streaming session, and the new mode takes effect immediately for all subsequent tool requests.

choices.text: Add `Edit` and `Write` to `disallowed_tools` for the rest of the session
choices.reason: A bare `disallowed_tools` entry removes the tool from the request, so Claude could no longer edit files at all.

choices.text: Call `set_permission_mode("acceptEdits")` on the client
choices.reason: Correct: the new mode takes effect immediately for all subsequent tool requests, so you can loosen permissions after reviewing Claude's approach.

choices.text: Call `set_permission_mode("plan")` so edits follow the approved plan
choices.reason: Plan mode is the opposite: file edits are never auto-approved there and prompt through your `canUseTool` callback.

takeaway: Start restrictive and loosen as trust builds: **`set_permission_mode()`** changes the mode mid-session for every later tool request.
explanation: Permission modes can change **during a streaming session**, and the new mode applies immediately to every later tool request. So once the user approves the approach, calling `set_permission_mode("acceptEdits")` on the client loosens edits for the rest of the session (Option C). Option A is the tempting trap, but restarting is unnecessary and throws away the session. Option B would remove Edit and Write from the request entirely, and D is the opposite of the goal, since plan mode never auto-approves edits.

stem: Your main SDK session runs in `bypassPermissions` inside a container. A reviewer subagent's `AgentDefinition` sets `permissionMode: "default"`, so you expect its risky tool calls to still need approval. What actually happens?

choices.text: It runs in `default`, because a subagent's own definition always wins over its parent
choices.reason: A subagent runs in the parent's mode unless its `permissionMode` is set **and** the parent is in `default`, `dontAsk` or `plan` mode.

choices.text: It runs in `bypassPermissions`; its own mode applies only under some parent modes
choices.reason: Correct: its `permissionMode` counts only when the parent is in `default`, `dontAsk` or `plan`; inheriting `bypassPermissions` grants full system access.

choices.text: It runs in `dontAsk`, so anything that would prompt is denied in the subagent
choices.reason: Nothing switches the subagent to `dontAsk`; with a `bypassPermissions` parent it simply runs in the parent's mode.

choices.text: It runs in `plan`, since review subagents are kept from editing by default
choices.reason: There is no such default; a subagent runs in the parent session's permission mode unless an allowed override applies.

takeaway: A subagent's own `permissionMode` applies only under a `default`, `dontAsk` or `plan` parent; under **`bypassPermissions`** it inherits full access.
explanation: A subagent's own `permissionMode` counts **only when the parent is in `default`, `dontAsk` or `plan`**; otherwise it runs in the parent's mode. The key detail is the parent's `bypassPermissions`, so the reviewer inherits it and gets full system access despite its `default` setting (Option B). Option A is the trap, assuming the subagent's definition always wins. Option C invents a switch to `dontAsk`, and D invents a default plan mode for review subagents; neither exists.

stem: Your web app runs one Agent SDK conversation per customer, all from the same working directory. When a customer returns the next day, their follow-up must land in their own earlier conversation. What should you do?

choices.text: Pass `continue: true`, which picks up the session automatically with no ID handling
choices.reason: `continue` resumes the most recent session in the current directory, which may belong to another customer; it suits one conversation at a time.

choices.text: Store each customer's `session_id` from the result message and pass it to `resume`
choices.reason: Correct: resume takes a specific session ID, which is required when you have multiple sessions, such as one per user in a multi-user app.

choices.text: Set `persistSession: false` so each customer's conversation is kept in memory
choices.reason: With `persistSession: false` the session exists only in memory for the duration of the call, so there is nothing to return to next day.

choices.text: Fork the customer's earlier session so the follow-up keeps their whole history
choices.reason: A fork is a new session with a copy of the history; the original stays unchanged, so the follow-up wouldn't land in that conversation.

takeaway: Many sessions in one place → store each **`session_id`** and pass it to `resume`; `continue` only finds the most recent one.
explanation: When many sessions live in one working directory, you need to name the exact one: store each customer's `session_id` from the result message and pass it to `resume` (Option B). Option A is the tempting shortcut, but `continue` resumes the **most recent** session in the directory, which may belong to another customer; it suits one conversation at a time. Option C keeps the session only in memory for the call, so nothing survives to the next day, and D creates a new forked session, leaving the original conversation untouched.

stem: You fork an SDK session so the agent can try an OAuth2 rewrite while you keep the original JWT thread. The forked agent edits `auth.ts`. When you resume the original session, `auth.ts` already contains the OAuth2 edits. Why?

choices.text: The fork reused the original's session ID, so both threads wrote to one history
choices.reason: A fork gets its own session ID, and the original's ID and history stay unchanged; the histories were separate.

choices.text: Resuming replays the fork's tool calls into the original conversation
choices.reason: Resuming the original continues its own history; the fork did not modify it. The edits came from the shared directory.

choices.text: Resume restores files from the fork's latest snapshot of the working directory
choices.reason: Sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem; nothing is restored on resume.

choices.text: Forks branch the conversation, not the files; file checkpointing can revert them
choices.reason: Correct: a forked agent's file edits are real and visible to any session in the same directory; use file checkpointing to snapshot and revert them.

takeaway: Sessions and forks branch the **conversation**, not the files; use file checkpointing to snapshot and revert file changes.
explanation: Sessions and forks branch the **conversation**, not the files. The forked agent's edits to `auth.ts` were real and landed in the shared directory, so any session there sees them; file checkpointing is the tool for snapshotting and reverting (Option D). Option A is the tempting explanation, but a fork gets its own session ID and the histories stayed separate. Option B is wrong because resuming continues the original's own history, and C fails because sessions persist the conversation and restore no files.

stem: You move a coding script from `claude -p` to the Python Agent SDK and don't set `system_prompt`. The agent now lacks Claude Code's usual tool guidance and safety behavior. What explains this, and what restores the CLI's behavior?

choices.text: The SDK's default prompt is minimal; set the `claude_code` preset
choices.reason: Correct: unset, the SDK uses a minimal prompt without the preset's security and safety instructions, unlike `claude -p`; the preset restores them.

choices.text: CLAUDE.md stopped loading; add `setting_sources=["project"]` to the options
choices.reason: Default `query()` options already load CLAUDE.md, and CLAUDE.md is injected into the conversation; it never replaces the system prompt.

choices.text: The SDK always uses the CLI prompt, so a model change must be the cause
choices.reason: It doesn't: unset, the SDK uses a minimal default that differs from the Claude Code system prompt `claude -p` uses.

choices.text: Put the CLI's prompt text into `append`, leaving out the preset type
choices.reason: `append` adds your text after the `claude_code` preset; it's set on the preset object, not a way to rebuild the CLI prompt.

takeaway: With no `system_prompt`, the SDK uses a **minimal** prompt; set the `claude_code` preset to match `claude -p`.
explanation: With `system_prompt` unset, the SDK uses a **minimal** default prompt, not the Claude Code prompt that `claude -p` uses, so the preset's security and safety instructions are missing. Setting the `claude_code` preset restores the CLI's behavior (Option A). Option B is the tempting trap, but default `query()` options already load CLAUDE.md, and it is injected into the conversation rather than replacing the system prompt. Option C wrongly assumes the SDK always uses the CLI prompt, and D misuses `append`, which only adds text after the preset.

stem: You're building an IDE-like coding tool where a developer watches and steers Claude. You want everything Claude Code's own system prompt provides, plus your company's coding standards. Which option is the lowest-risk customization?

choices.text: A custom `systemPrompt` string that contains your coding standards
choices.reason: A custom string sends only what you write, so you take responsibility for replacing the tool guidance and safety instructions.

choices.text: No `systemPrompt` at all, with the standards in each user prompt
choices.reason: The minimal default covers tool calling but omits the rest of the preset, including its security and safety instructions.

choices.text: The `claude_code` preset, with your standards added in `append`
choices.reason: Correct: you get the Claude Code prompt with your instructions added after it. Nothing is removed, so it's the lowest-risk customization.

choices.text: An output style holding your standards, without `keep-coding-instructions`
choices.reason: A custom output style leaves the preset's software engineering instructions out unless you set `keep-coding-instructions: true`.

takeaway: Want Claude Code's behavior plus your rules? Use the **`claude_code` preset with `append`**: nothing is removed.
explanation: The goal is **everything** Claude Code's prompt provides **plus** your standards, so the safest move is the one that removes nothing: the `claude_code` preset with your standards in `append` (Option C). Option A is the tempting trap, because a custom `systemPrompt` sends only what you write, leaving you responsible for replacing tool guidance and safety instructions. Option B's minimal default also omits the preset's safety instructions, and D's output style drops the software engineering instructions unless `keep-coding-instructions: true` is set.

stem: Midway through a long session in your production SDK app, your user switches the agent to read-only. You resume the session with a new `append` saying the workspace is read-only, but Claude keeps proposing edits. How should you get the instruction to Claude on the next turn?

choices.text: Send it in your next user message, or as hook `additionalContext`
choices.reason: Correct: the recorded prompt is reused until compaction, so send changes in the conversation, e.g. via a `UserPromptSubmit` hook's `additionalContext`.

choices.text: Pass the new `append` again on each resume until Claude picks it up
choices.reason: A different `append` on a resumed session isn't seen: the prompt recorded on the first request is reused until the session is compacted.

choices.text: Turn prompt recording off with `snapshot: false` in production
choices.reason: The docs say to keep recording on in production: with it off, the changed prompt can't reuse the session's prompt cache.

choices.text: Replace `append` with a custom prompt string, which is never recorded
choices.reason: Custom strings are recorded too: a different `append` or custom prompt on resume isn't seen until compaction or a new session.

takeaway: A session reuses its recorded system prompt until compaction; send mid-session changes **in the conversation** (next message or hook `additionalContext`).
explanation: A session reuses the system prompt **recorded on its first request** until compaction, so a new `append` on resume is never seen. Mid-session changes must travel **in the conversation**: your next user message, or `additionalContext` from a hook such as `UserPromptSubmit` (Option A). Option B is the tempting retry, but repeating `append` hits the same recorded prompt. Option D fails because custom strings are recorded too, and C is discouraged in production because turning recording off stops the changed prompt from reusing the prompt cache.

stem: Your SDK agent should follow the repo's CLAUDE.md, the same file developers use interactively. A teammate set `settingSources: []` to keep host settings out, and now the agent ignores the project conventions. What's the fix?

choices.text: Pass `skills: "all"`, so the CLAUDE.md conventions load on demand
choices.reason: The `skills` option picks which discovered skills are enabled; CLAUDE.md loads through setting sources, and with `[]` the project isn't read.

choices.text: Set `settingSources: ["local"]`, which loads instructions for this checkout
choices.reason: `local` loads `CLAUDE.local.md` and `settings.local.json`, not the project's shared CLAUDE.md.

choices.text: Re-enable auto memory with `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=0` in `env`
choices.reason: Auto memory is a separate input read regardless of `settingSources`; it isn't where the project CLAUDE.md comes from.

choices.text: Set `settingSources: ["project"]` to load the project CLAUDE.md and rules
choices.reason: Correct: the `project` source loads project CLAUDE.md and `.claude/rules/*.md`, sharing context between interactive sessions and the SDK.

takeaway: CLAUDE.md and `.claude/rules/` load through **`settingSources`**; `[]` turns off user, project and local settings, including them.
explanation: CLAUDE.md and `.claude/rules/*.md` load through **setting sources**, and `settingSources: []` turns off user, project and local settings, which is why the conventions vanished. Adding back only the `project` source restores the shared CLAUDE.md while still keeping host settings out (Option D). Option B is the closest trap, but `local` loads `CLAUDE.local.md` and `settings.local.json`, not the project's shared file. Option A only picks enabled skills, and C's auto memory is a separate input, not where the project CLAUDE.md comes from.

source.title: Use Claude Code features in the SDK

stem: You host an Agent SDK service where each request runs for a different customer tenant. One tenant's agent must not pick up host-level configuration or another tenant's per-directory memory. Which steps does the documentation recommend?

choices.text: Keep default `query()` options, which already isolate each tenant's settings
choices.reason: The docs warn not to rely on default options for multi-tenant isolation: some inputs are read regardless of `settingSources`.

choices.text: Run each tenant in its own filesystem
choices.reason: Correct: the docs say to run each tenant in its own filesystem, because an SDK process can otherwise pick up per-directory memory.

choices.text: Set `settingSources: []` and `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` in `env`
choices.reason: Correct: `[]` turns off user, project and local settings, and the variable turns off auto memory, which `settingSources` doesn't control.

choices.text: Pass `mcpServers: {}` so no claude.ai connectors can load for a tenant
choices.reason: Passing `mcpServers: {}` does not suppress claude.ai connectors; that takes `strictMcpConfig` or another documented switch.

choices.text: Leave `"user"` out of `settingSources` so `~/.claude.json` is skipped
choices.reason: The global `~/.claude.json` config is always read; it can only be relocated with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`.

takeaway: Defaults are not tenant isolation: give each tenant **its own filesystem**, and set `settingSources: []` plus `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1`.
explanation: Defaults do not isolate tenants, because some inputs are read regardless of `settingSources`. So the docs recommend **its own filesystem** per tenant (B), since an SDK process can otherwise pick up per-directory memory, plus `settingSources: []` with `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` (C) to turn off settings and the auto memory that settings sources don't control. Option E is the most tempting wrong pick: `~/.claude.json` is always read and can only be relocated with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. Option D does not suppress claude.ai connectors, and A relies on defaults.

source.title: Use Claude Code features in the SDK

stem: You register an SDK `PreToolUse` hook with the matcher `"\.env$"` to block edits to env files. It never fires, even when Claude edits `.env`. What should you change?

choices.text: Move the hook to `PostToolUse`, whose matcher is tested against file paths
choices.reason: Tool-based hooks match the tool name in every case, and `PostToolUse` runs after the write has already happened.

choices.text: Match `Write|Edit`, then check `tool_input.file_path` inside the callback
choices.reason: Correct: matchers only match tool names, not file paths or other arguments; filter by path inside the hook.

choices.text: Remove the matcher, since a hook with no matcher skips the file-editing tools
choices.reason: The reverse: a hook without a matcher runs for every event of that type, file-editing tools included.

choices.text: Return an async output so the hook can inspect the file before it's written
choices.reason: Async outputs can't block, modify or inject context, because the agent has already moved on.

takeaway: Hook matchers test the **tool name**; filter on paths or other arguments inside the callback via `tool_input`.
explanation: Tool-based hook matchers are tested against the **tool name** only, never file paths or other arguments, so `"\.env$"` matches nothing. Match `Write|Edit` and check `tool_input.file_path` inside the callback (Option B). Option A is the tempting fix, but `PostToolUse` matches tool names too, and it runs after the write already happened. Option C has it backwards (no matcher means the hook runs for every event of that type), and D's async output cannot block anything because the agent has already moved on.

source.title: Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks

stem: Your SDK agent should only ever write files under `./sandbox`. Instead of blocking writes elsewhere, you want them redirected there automatically. What should your `PreToolUse` hook for `Write` return?

choices.text: A top-level `updatedInput` carrying the rewritten `file_path`
choices.reason: `updatedInput` must sit inside `hookSpecificOutput`, not at the top level, or the modified input isn't applied.

choices.text: A `systemMessage` telling Claude to write under `./sandbox` instead
choices.reason: `systemMessage` shows a message to the user; it doesn't change the tool call's input.

choices.text: `updatedInput` with the new path in `hookSpecificOutput`, plus `allow`
choices.reason: Correct: `updatedInput` rewrites the call, and pairing it with `permissionDecision: "allow"` auto-approves the rewritten operation.

choices.text: `updatedInput` with the new path and `permissionDecision: "defer"`
choices.reason: With `defer`, `updatedInput` is ignored, and the turn ends with `stop_reason` `"tool_deferred"`.

takeaway: To change what a tool does, return **`updatedInput`** inside `hookSpecificOutput`, with `allow` to auto-approve it; `defer` drops it.
explanation: To **rewrite** a tool call rather than block it, return `updatedInput` inside `hookSpecificOutput`, and pair it with `permissionDecision: "allow"` so the rewritten write is auto-approved (Option C). Option A is the subtle trap: the right field in the wrong place, since a top-level `updatedInput` is not applied. Option D fails because with `defer` the `updatedInput` is ignored and the turn ends with `stop_reason` `"tool_deferred"`. Option B's `systemMessage` only shows the user a message and changes nothing about the call.

source.title: Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks

stem: Your own agent loop on the Messages API enables the server-executed `web_search` tool. A research request comes back with `stop_reason: "pause_turn"` and no final answer. What should your loop do next?

choices.text: Treat the turn as finished and return the text that came back so far
choices.reason: A paused turn means the work isn't finished; the model was still iterating when it hit the server loop's cap.

choices.text: Run the searches yourself and send the output back in `tool_result` blocks
choices.reason: Anthropic runs server-executed tools; you never construct a `tool_result` block for them.

choices.text: Re-send the conversation, including the paused response, to let it continue
choices.reason: Correct: re-sending the conversation with the paused response lets the model continue where it left off.

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` and send only the original user message again
choices.reason: `pause_turn` comes from the server-side loop's iteration limit, not output length, and dropping the paused response loses its progress.

takeaway: `pause_turn` means the server-side loop hit its iteration cap: **re-send** the conversation, paused response included, to continue.
explanation: `pause_turn` means the server-side loop for server-executed tools hit its **iteration cap** while the model was still working, so the turn is not finished. Re-send the conversation **including the paused response** and the model continues where it left off (Option C). Option D is the tempting trap: it treats the pause as an output-length problem and drops the paused response, losing progress. Option A returns an unfinished answer, and B is wrong because Anthropic runs server-executed tools, so you never build `tool_result` blocks for them.

diagram.caption: A paused server-tool turn continues when you re-send it.

stem: Your team wants fine-grained control over its agent: how each step runs, when tools execute and how results are fed back. It is happy to build and run the loop itself. Which approach does Anthropic's documentation match to this need?

choices.text: Claude Managed Agents, configured with your own agent definition
choices.reason: Managed Agents is a pre-built harness, best for long-running tasks and asynchronous work, used instead of building your own loop.

choices.text: The Messages API, with an agent loop you build and run yourself
choices.reason: Correct: the docs list the Messages API as best for custom agent loops and fine-grained control, with direct model access.

choices.text: Claude Managed Agents with a self-hosted sandbox environment
choices.reason: A self-hosted sandbox only changes where sessions run; the agent still uses Managed Agents' pre-built harness.

choices.text: A Managed Agents scheduled deployment that runs on a cron schedule
choices.reason: Scheduled deployments are for recurring agent runs on a cron schedule; they don't give step-level control of the loop.

takeaway: Messages API = **custom loops and fine-grained control**; Managed Agents = pre-built harness for long-running, asynchronous work.
explanation: The stem's need is **fine-grained control** over each step, when tools run and how results feed back, with a team willing to build the loop itself. The docs match that to the Messages API with your own agent loop (Option B). Option C is the tempting trap because self-hosting sounds like more control, but it only changes where sessions run; the pre-built harness still drives the loop. Option A is that same pre-built harness for long-running, asynchronous work, and D only schedules recurring runs on cron.

stem: A bank adopts Claude Managed Agents with a self-hosted sandbox so its agent can reach internal services that aren't publicly routable. Which statements about this setup are accurate?

choices.text: Your environment worker runs each tool call locally and posts the result back
choices.reason: Correct: Claude requests tool calls and your worker, a process on your infrastructure, runs each one locally and posts the result back.

choices.text: Claude itself runs on the worker host, so no prompt leaves the bank's network
choices.reason: Claude runs on Anthropic's side; self-hosting moves tool execution, not the model, into your infrastructure.

choices.text: The model is configured on the self-hosted environment, not on the agent
choices.reason: The model is configured on the agent, not the environment; self-hosted sandboxes support every model available in Managed Agents.

choices.text: The worker must accept inbound HTTPS from Anthropic to receive new work
choices.reason: The worker claims work items from a queue and needs only outbound HTTPS.

choices.text: Tool inputs and outputs still flow to Anthropic's control plane
choices.reason: Correct: tool inputs and outputs still flow to Anthropic's control plane, so the model can see results and decide what to do next.

takeaway: Self-hosted sandboxes move **tool execution** to your worker; orchestration and the model stay on Anthropic's side, and tool I/O still flows there.
explanation: A self-hosted sandbox moves **tool execution** into the bank's network, nothing more. Claude requests tool calls, the worker runs each one locally and posts the result back (A), and those tool inputs and outputs still flow to Anthropic's control plane so the model can decide its next step (E). Option B is the most tempting wrong pick: Claude itself still runs on Anthropic's side. Option C misplaces the model setting (it lives on the agent), and D is wrong because the worker claims work from a queue with only outbound HTTPS.

diagram.caption: Orchestration stays with Anthropic; tools run on your worker.

stem: A Claude Managed Agents session is partway through a long data-cleanup task when you realise it should skip the archive tables. What does the documented workflow let you do?

choices.text: Nothing until it finishes; then start a new session with corrected instructions
choices.reason: You don't have to wait: the workflow lets you guide a running session with more user events or interrupt it.

choices.text: Fetch the session's event history and edit the earlier user turn in place
choices.reason: Event history is persisted server-side and can be fetched in full, but you steer by sending new events, not by rewriting history.

choices.reason: Correct: you can send additional user events to guide the agent mid-execution, or interrupt it to change direction.
